extra.message: Hardcoded Application Secret Key — Session forgery — attacker can craft arbitrary Flask session cookies to impersonate any user (including admin) and bypass CSRF protection globally. [verified: SECRET_KEY is hardcoded as 'secure-secret-key-12345' in source (line 25); anyone with source access can forge Flask session cookies and CSRF tokens.]

SQL Injection in Login — Authentication bypass — attacker can log in as any user (including admin) without knowing the password, gaining full access to the application. [verified: Username and password from LoginForm are interpolated via f-string directly into a SQL query with no parameterization (line 163–168); form.validate_on_submit() only checks DataRequired, providing zero SQL injection prevention.]

Unrestricted File Upload — Remote code execution via web shell upload, serving phishing pages, or malware distribution from the trusted domain. [verified: No file extension or content-type validation; files are saved directly to static/uploads/ and served via /uploads/<filename>; the route is also CSRF-exempt.]

Insecure Deserialization via pickle.loads — Remote code execution — attacker can execute arbitrary Python code on the server, leading to complete server compromise. [verified: User-supplied base64 data is decoded and passed directly to pickle.loads() (line ~434) with no validation, enabling arbitrary code execution on the server.]

Debug Mode Enabled in Production — Remote code execution via Werkzeug debugger console, source code disclosure via debug tracebacks, and information leakage. [verified: app.run(host='0.0.0.0', debug=True) (line 661) exposes the Werkzeug debugger console to the network, enabling interactive code execution on exceptions.]

SQL Injection in Comment Search — Data exfiltration — attacker can read all database tables including users table with passwords and emails. [verified: search_term from CommentSearchForm is interpolated via f-string into a SQL LIKE clause with no parameterization (line ~246); no sanitization or escaping exists, enabling data exfiltration.]

Cross-Site Request Forgery via GET on Transfer — Unauthorized state-changing actions performed on behalf of the victim — progress manipulation and log pollution. [verified: GET /transfer?amount=<int> triggers database writes (progress update, log_action) without any CSRF token check; GET-based state change is inherently CSRF-vulnerable.]

Missing CSRF Protection on File Upload — Cross-origin file uploads on behalf of authenticated users, enabling malware hosting or phishing attacks. [verified: /upload is decorated with @csrf.exempt, disabling Flask-WTF CSRF protection on a state-changing endpoint that saves files and updates progress.]

Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) — Access to internal services and cloud metadata endpoints, potential lateral movement within the network. [verified: URL from SSRFForm is passed to requests.get() with no allowlist or validation (line ~383); attacker can target internal services and cloud metadata endpoints.]

Broken Object-Level Authorization (BOLA) in API — Unauthorized API access to all users' PII — usernames, emails, and roles exposed programmatically, enabling bulk data harvesting. [verified: /api/user/<int:user_id> returns JSON with any user's id, username, email, and role based solely on the URL parameter; no authorization check exists beyond session presence.]

Missing CSRF Protection on /reset/<page> Endpoints — Cross-site request forgery can cause authenticated users to unwittingly delete all comments, all uploaded files, or their own progress/reports, leading to data loss across the application [verified: The /reset/<page> POST route uses no FlaskForm and performs no CSRF token validation; CSRFProtect only checks when a form is instantiated, so destructive operations (DELETE FROM comments, shutil.rmtree of all uploads) are reachable via cross-site requests from an authenticated victim.]

Missing Authorization — Any Authenticated User Can Delete All Comments and Uploads — Any authenticated user can delete all comments and all uploaded files in the application, enabling data loss and denial of service against all other users [verified: The /reset/<page> handler checks session['user'] (authentication) but has zero role or ownership check; any authenticated user can issue DELETE FROM comments or shutil.rmtree(UPLOAD_FOLDER), destroying data globally regardless of who owns it.]

Missing rate limiting on authentication endpoint enabling brute-force attacks — An attacker can automate credential guessing against the login endpoint to compromise user accounts, including the admin account (password 'password'), gaining full administrative access to the application. [verified: No rate limiting, account lockout, or CAPTCHA exists on the /login endpoint; weak default credentials (admin:password) make brute-force trivial.]

Predictable Session Token Generation — Session hijacking and privilege escalation — attacker can guess admin session ID (admin_auth_123) and impersonate the admin user. [verified: Session tokens follow a predictable format (username_auth_123) stored in both the Flask session and a cookie; the format is trivially guessable for any known username.]

Insecure Cookie Flags (Missing Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite) — Session cookie theft via network sniffing (no Secure) or XSS (no HttpOnly), and CSRF amplification (no SameSite). [verified: set_cookie('vuln_session_id', ...) omits Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite flags, exposing the cookie to network interception, JavaScript access, and cross-site requests.]

Missing Authentication on Uploaded File Access — Unauthenticated users can access all uploaded files, including potentially malicious content or sensitive data uploaded by other users [verified: The /uploads/<filename> route has no session authentication check at all—unlike virtually every other route—and returns any file from UPLOAD_FOLDER via send_from_directory; the same files are also reachable unauthenticated via the /static/<path:filename> passthrough.]

Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) in Profile — Unauthorized access to other users' PII including email addresses and roles, enabling targeted phishing or privilege escalation intelligence. [verified: Any authenticated user can view any other user's profile by changing the URL parameter; no ownership or role check prevents access to PII including email and role.]

Missing CSRF Protection on /broken-auth Endpoint — Attacker can force a logged-in victim to complete the broken-auth challenge and update progress without user intent; combined with predictable session tokens, attacker can craft a fully successful CSRF exploit [verified: The /broken-auth POST route reads request.form.get('session_token') directly with no FlaskForm instantiated, so Flask-WTF CSRFProtect never enforces a token check for this handler even though CSRFProtect(app) is initialized globally; the predictable session_id format (username_auth_123) makes the CSRF exploit feasible.]

Missing CSRF Protection on Settings Update — Unauthorized email changes on behalf of authenticated users via cross-origin requests. [verified: /csrf route is decorated with @csrf.exempt and performs state changes (update_progress) without any CSRF token enforcement.]

Sensitive Data Exposure — Unauthenticated Flag API — CTF challenge bypass — attackers can obtain challenge flags without completing the associated challenges, undermining the scoring system. [verified: /api/flag returns a hardcoded CTF flag with no authentication check; any unauthenticated user can retrieve the flag directly.]

Plaintext Password Storage in Database Schema — All user passwords are stored in plaintext in the SQLite database; if the database file is accessed via path traversal, backup exposure, or SSRF to file://, all credentials are immediately usable [verified: The `users` table schema at database.py:51 defines `password TEXT NOT NULL` with zero hashing infrastructure — no import or use of bcrypt/PBKDF2/hashlib for password storage anywhere in the project source. Passwords (admin:password, user2:password2) are inserted and compared in plaintext (app.py:165). The SQLite database is reachable via SSRF file://, XXE file://, or direct filesystem access per t]

Default Hardcoded Credentials in Database Seed — Unauthorized administrative access — anyone can log in as admin using the well-known password 'password', gaining full access to the application. [verified: database.py:97-99 seeds users ('admin','password') and ('user2','password2') via INSERT OR IGNORE; init_db() runs at startup and the login endpoint accepts these credentials. No forced-password-change, no password policy, and the admin role is set but never checked anywhere (is_admin is written to session at app.py:183 but read by zero routes/templates), limiting impact to unauthorized account acc]

Missing Authentication on /comments-log Endpoint — Unauthenticated users can read the internal comments log file, potentially exposing application data [verified: The /comments-log route has no session check and reads static/comments.txt directly, returning its contents to anyone without authentication; the exposed data is internal app commentary, not highly sensitive, but the control is genuinely absent.]
